subject: Mesh hotspots, extrapolation of the local trend?

messages.author: 7a4a5fe753932e1a
messages.subject: Mesh hotspots, extrapolation of the local trend?
parts:
Dear R-INLA forum,

I' m modelling (log) daily particulate matter concentrations (PM10) over Italy. My problem is the occurance of strange hotspots in the predicted maps. The problem is not related to the selected covariates, as the hotspots appear even in a model with only Intercept plus spde. I tried different approaches to build the mesh, but with no success. I think the problem does not depend on the mesh construction, but on the clusterization of the points stations.

I attach some plots to show my problem.

The plot with the mesh for Italy (blu - yellow gradient) is the average spde over the month of June 2015. The hotspot is visible in the upper-left side of the mesh (I attach a zoom on this area). The plot with the terrain gradient shows the same hotspot for a casual day during the winter season. In this case the model was run over the North of Italy alone with a finer mesh.

The only solution to my problem is to filter out the stations which are to close to one another, in order to avoid a cluster in the proximity of the hotspot. However: 1) other hotspots are still visibile in the winter time mesh (not shown); 2) I cannot drop the stations from the input dataset without any clear explaination.

Something similar to my problem is described in the post titled "What could be the cause of hot/cold spots outside the sample area in the posterior mean spatial GMRF". As suggeted by Finn in that post, i could think that the hotspot is due to the extrapolation of the local trend in an area without data. Do you have a sugggestion on how one could solve this problem?

Below, I attach the code.

The estimated range is ~ 200 km (in winter time) and ~400 km in summer time.

Follow the summary for the hyper-parameters (whole Italy, January and February 2015):

Summary hyper

##                                                mean           sd  0.025quant
## Precision for the Gaussian observations  24.5787498  0.540503065  23.5449281
## Precision for wday                      116.5821332 80.150231828  23.8149808
## Range for i                             203.8083427  8.337874614 186.8624183
## Stdev for i                               1.5654533  0.139321354   1.2695627
## GroupRho for i                            0.9677393  0.006123818   0.9526211
##                                            0.5quant  0.975quant        mode
## Precision for the Gaussian observations  24.5681879  25.6660343  24.5406367
## Precision for wday                       97.3759464 322.7531155  61.8834170
## Range for i                             204.1092230 219.4444598 205.4184501
## Stdev for i                               1.5778139   1.8030952   1.6322248
## GroupRho for i                            0.9690276   0.9759526   0.9722952


The code (the relevant part of the code only):



######################## Model FORMULA: Intercept+SPDE
as.formula(lpm10~Intercept-1)->myformula
########################


#Mesh construction: EPSG: 32632 (in kilometers)
 
inla.nonconvex.hull(pointsTrainingPoints)->ppp
 mesh<-inla.mesh.2d(boundary  = ppp, max.edge = c(30,100),cutoff=5,offset=c(10),min.angle=25)

#CONSTR=FALSE does not affect the results
inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh=mesh,alpha=2,constr=TRUE,prior.range = c(150,0.8),prior.sigma = c(0.8,0.2))->spde
inla.spde.make.index(name="i",n.spde=spde$n.spde,n.group = n_giorni)->iset #n_giorni: number of days in the period

...stack...

#Pc.priors:

list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.1)))->prec_hyper
list(prior="pc.cor1",param=c(0.8,0.318))->theta_hyper

#Update the formula with the random effects:
#wday is the day of the week

update(myformula,.~.+f(wday,model="rw1",hyper=prec_hyper,cyclic = FALSE)+f(i,model=spde,group = i.group,control.group = list(model="ar1",hyper=list(theta=theta_hyper))))->myformula

inla(myformula,
     data=inla.stack.data(mystack,spde=spde),
     family ="gaussian",
     verbose=TRUE,
     control.compute = list(openmp.strategy="pardiso.parallel",cpo=TRUE,waic=TRUE,dic=TRUE,config=TRUE),
     control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0.001, prec=1,mean.intercept=0),
     control.predictor =list(A=inla.stack.A(mystack),compute=TRUE) )->>inla.out


Thanks in advance for your attention and suggestions.

Guido

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Mesh hotspots, extrapolation of the local trend?
parts:
Yes,
The sharp spots look very much like local extrapolation effects, and in fact one can see that effect to a lesser degree outside most of the data-dense regions in your plots.
One important thing to keep in mind is that the posterior mean doesn’t tell the whole story. First thing should be to look at the credible prediction intervals for the field; if the upper bounds are extra high at the low hotspots and extra low at the high hotspots, the result just sows that the values are uncertain there.
Howeve, it may be that your model doesn’t pick up on local issues with the data, and overfits. No really universal way to solve that except “improve the model structure”, and “consider the priors more carefully”.

Finn

parts:
Dear Finn,

as you suggested I checked the spde quantiles and they confirm that the observed hotspot is the result of an overfitting problem.

As I have no further covariates to explain the local PM10 variability, I have added a random effect (iid model) on the stations points. The use of a random effect component does not seem to alter considerably the parameters estimates (the range without random effects was ~400 km and now 300 km, the group rho was ~0.9 now 0.7), as well as the (good) model performance on both the training and validation datasets. Most importantly, the associated spde does not show any strange hotspot.

Two questions:

1) Do you think that this approach (the random effect on the stations points) to overcome the overfitting problem is good or not? Obviously, my model does not capture local PM10 variability, but it looks good for describing the PM10 variability on the whole country;

2) The PIT histogram shows a humpback-shape, but the model validation gives good results: how much attention should I pay to the PIT shape to judge my model ?

Thanks
Guido



Guido
